label: Claude Opus 5.5
output:
Croydon. 11 November.

Kelechi,

You said put it in writing. So here it is, in an envelope, with a stamp, like it's 1997. Read it on the train. Don't pretend you've read it when you've only read the first paragraph, I know you.

First, let me remind you of something. Moremi, second year, the week before the MTH 201 exam. Who was sitting on the floor of the common room at 1am with a biro and the back of someone's handout, explaining eigenvalues to six people who had given up on life? Not me. I was one of the six. You explained it three different ways until Tunde got it, and Tunde was not a serious person. You didn't make anybody feel stupid. You just kept going until it clicked, and then you made a joke about Tunde's head and we all went to sleep happy.

That's the whole job, Kelechi. That's teaching. You were doing it for free in a hostel with no light half the time.

Now look at what you're doing with that brain. Nine years checking other people's costings. You told me at my birthday that every day is the same spreadsheet. You said it like a joke but your face wasn't joking. And on your own birthday last year you said, "I just want to do something that matters before 40." You probably don't remember saying it because you'd had two glasses of wine, but I remember. You're 34. That's six years. A training year and five years of actually doing the thing. The maths works, and you of all people can't argue with the maths.

So let me tell you what I actually want, because I'm not asking you to resign tomorrow. I'm asking you to come to an open evening.

Thursday 19 November, 6pm, at the training partnership in Lewisham. That's next week. It's not far from you. I'll come with you. You can sit there with your arms folded and your sceptical face, ask them hard questions about money, and then I'll buy you suya after. You don't sign anything. You just listen. If you walk out and say "no, this is not for me," fine, I'll never mention it again. (That's a lie. I'll mention it at your 40th. But only once.)

The route I'm talking about is the salaried one. You get paid while you train. It's one year, you're in a school from the start, and if you apply this round you'd start September 2027. So you're not going back to being a student eating Indomie. You're working, you're earning, you're learning on the job.

Now, the honest part, because I know if I only tell you the sweet things you'll think I've joined a cult.

The pay drops in the first year. I won't dress it up. You'll feel it. It goes up after, and there's the pension (which is actually very good, I didn't appreciate it until I compared with my cousin's), and there are the holidays, which yes, everybody jokes about, but when you're in the middle of term you understand why they exist. Still, year one, your account will be quieter than it is now. Plan for it.

The marking never ends. Never. You finish one pile and another one has grown behind you like Nollywood juju. Some days behaviour is pure wahala. Some days a Year 8 class will test you like you owe them money. You'll have lessons that go badly and you'll replay them in your head at night.

And because I said I'd be honest: when I started in 2019, I cried in the school car park. Twice. First term. Sat in my car with the engine off and just let it out, then wiped my face and drove home. I'm not ashamed of that and I'm not telling you to scare you. I'm telling you because it got better. Properly better. By the second year I was a different person. The first term is the hardest, and everybody who's honest will tell you the same thing.

So that's the bad side. Now hear the other side.

Last month I had a Year 11 boy, Damola. Three weeks we'd been on simultaneous equations. Three weeks of him staring at the board like it insulted his mother. Then one Tuesday, in the middle of a question, something just turned over in his head and he shouted, "IS THAT ALL??" Kelechi, the whole class clapped. Spontaneously. Year 11 boys, clapping for maths. Damola was standing up like he'd scored a penalty. I went to the staff room afterwards and just sat there smiling like a mumu. You don't get that from a spreadsheet. I promise you, no cost report has ever made a room full of sixteen-year-olds clap.

And don't tell me you're not good with kids. My nephew still talks about Christmas. "Uncle Kelechi and the jollof." You sat at that table and taught a nine-year-old fractions using jollof rice portions on plates, half a plate, a quarter plate, "if I take this piece, what's left?" He gets fractions now. His teacher said he suddenly gets it. He thinks you're a genius. He also thinks you're funny, which is debatable, but kids are generous.

That's the thing about you. You're patient, you're funny, and you explain things without making people feel small. Those three things together are rarer than you think. I've seen people with first-class maths degrees who cannot teach a child to save their life, because they get impatient, or they make the kid feel slow. You don't do that. You never did. It's the reason half of Moremi passed that exam.

And here's why I'm not just being sentimental. Our school, 1,100 kids in Peckham, has had a supply teacher covering two Year 9 maths groups since September. Two groups. That's around sixty children who don't have a permanent maths teacher this year. The supply teacher is trying, but he doesn't know their names properly and he won't be there next year. Those kids will sit GCSEs in two years. That's what "something that matters" looks like in real life. It's not abstract. It's sixty children in Peckham who need someone exactly like you.

Before you start: no, you're not too old. A woman in my department started training at 41. Forty-one. She's one of the best teachers we have, the kids respect her, and she brings everything from her old job into the classroom. Your nine years aren't wasted. You'll be the teacher who can answer "when will I ever use this?" with an actual answer from actual buildings. Kids love that.

I'll say this once and then leave it. You're wasting yourself. I say it with love. Checking other people's numbers is a skill, but it's not your gift. Your gift is making things make sense to other people. You've been doing it since we were nineteen. It's time you got paid for it.

So. Thursday 19 November. 6pm. Lewisham. I'll meet you at the station or wherever you want. Bring your hard questions. Bring your folded arms. Just come and hear them out. That's all I'm asking.

If after that you say no, I'll respect it. Mostly.

And yes, I know you're laughing that I actually posted this. Good. Keep it. When you're Head of Maths somewhere I'll ask for it back and frame it.

Your guy,
